data.title: Vishay Precision Group, Inc. Just Missed EPS By 54%: Here's What Analysts Think Will Happen Next
data.description:
There's been a notable change in appetite for Vishay Precision Group, Inc. (NYSE:VPG) shares in the week since its quarterly report, with the stock down 19% to US$44.21. It looks like a pretty bad result, all things considered. Although revenues of US$85m were in line with analyst predictions, statutory earnings fell badly short, missing estimates by 54% to hit US$0.04 per share. Following the result, the analysts have updated their earnings model, and it would be good to know whether they think there's been a strong change in the company's prospects, or if it's business as usual. We thought readers would find it interesting to see the analysts latest (statutory) post-earnings forecasts for next year.

Taking into account the latest results, the current consensus from Vishay Precision Group's three analysts is for revenues of US$370.8m in 2027. This would reflect a notable 11% increase on its revenue over the past 12 months. Earnings are expected to improve, with Vishay Precision Group forecast to report a statutory profit of US$1.62 per share. Yet prior to the latest earnings, the analysts had been anticipated revenues of US$370.8m and earnings per share (EPS) of US$1.62 in 2027. The consensus analysts don't seem to have seen anything in these results that would have changed their view on the business, given there's been no major change to their estimates.

There were no changes to revenue or earnings estimates or the price target of US$93.33, suggesting that the company has met expectations in its recent result. That's not the only conclusion we can draw from this data however, as some investors also like to consider the spread in estimates when evaluating analyst price targets. The most optimistic Vishay Precision Group analyst has a price target of US$105 per share, while the most pessimistic values it at US$77.00. Analysts definitely have varying views on the business, but the spread of estimates is not wide enough in our view to suggest that extreme outcomes could await Vishay Precision Group shareholders.

Looking at the bigger picture now, one of the ways we can make sense of these forecasts is to see how they measure up against both past performance and industry growth estimates. One thing stands out from these estimates, which is that Vishay Precision Group is forecast to grow faster in the future than it has in the past, with revenues expected to display 8.7% annualised growth until the end of 2027. If achieved, this would be a much better result than the 1.9% annual decline over the past five years. By contrast, our data suggests that other companies (with analyst coverage) in a similar industry are forecast to see their revenue grow 14% per year. Although Vishay Precision Group's revenues are expected to improve, it seems that the analysts are still bearish on the business, forecasting it to grow slower than the broader industry.

The Bottom Line

The most obvious conclusion is that there's been no major change in the business' prospects in recent times, with the analysts holding their earnings forecasts steady, in line with previous estimates. On the plus side, there were no major changes to revenue estimates; although forecasts imply they will perform worse than the wider industry. There was no real change to the consensus price target, suggesting that the intrinsic value of the business has not undergone any major changes with the latest estimates.

data.description:

What Skanska Investors Were Really Arguing About

The shares cost SEK249 at the start of the period, and the live question was whether Skanska’s order book and green credentials justified a richer story than the sticker price implied.

The bullish Narrative pointed to a Fair Value of SEK285, the price implied if strong assumptions proved right, built on Skanska’s long backlog and push into sustainable, higher margin projects. Supporters leaned on expectations for faster revenue growth and wider profit margins helped by digitalization and cost discipline.

The bearish Narrative anchored on a Fair Value of SEK210, again an implied price, shaped by worries over climate regulation and labor shortages. This view stressed the risk that rising project costs, demographic headwinds in parts of Europe, and dependence on big public contracts could limit revenue growth and keep profitability under pressure.

What The Results Changed For The Skanska Argument

The clearest new data point for Skanska was the Q3 2026 report, where revenue reached SEK46,409 million and net income was SEK1,266 million. Both lines were higher than a year earlier and the net margin ticked up from 2.5% to 2.7%. That nudged the story toward the optimistic camp on profitability, although the gain was small enough that it did not settle the debate.

The lesson to lift for any other contractor is simple. When a thesis rests on margin expansion, track the reported net margin quarter by quarter, not just the contract headlines or backlog size.

What Skanska’s Current Price Already Assumes

Skanska’s share price is now SEK288 after a 26.2% gain over the past year, while the selected Narrative’s Fair Value sits below the current price. That view leans on worries that strong civil and high tech construction work may not fully counter weaker areas.

Anyone paying SEK288 is effectively assuming Skanska’s record backlog can support resilient construction margins and earnings quality. The live question is how the highlighted Nordic housing softness and property impairments might challenge that belief.

data.title: Should You Buy ResMed Inc. (NYSE:RMD) For Its Upcoming Dividend?
data.description:
Regular readers will know that we love our dividends at Simply Wall St, which is why it's exciting to see ResMed Inc. (NYSE:RMD) is about to trade ex-dividend in the next 4 days. Typically, the ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the date on which a company determines the shareholders eligible to receive a dividend. It is important to be aware of the ex-dividend date because any trade on the stock needs to have been settled on or before the record date. Meaning, you will need to purchase ResMed's shares before the 12th of November to receive the dividend, which will be paid on the 17th of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$0.66 per share, and in the last 12 months, the company paid a total of US$2.64 per share. Last year's total dividend payments show that ResMed has a trailing yield of 1.1% on the current share price of US$235.30. If you buy this business for its dividend, you should have an idea of whether ResMed's dividend is reliable and sustainable. So we need to investigate whether ResMed can afford its dividend, and if the dividend could grow.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Dividends are typically paid from company earnings. If a company pays more in dividends than it earned in profit, then the dividend could be unsustainable. ResMed has a low and conservative payout ratio of just 22% of its income after tax. That said, even highly profitable companies sometimes might not generate enough cash to pay the dividend, which is why we should always check if the dividend is covered by cash flow. The good news is it paid out just 22% of its free cash flow in the last year.

It's encouraging to see that the dividend is covered by both profit and cash flow. This generally suggests the dividend is sustainable, as long as earnings don't drop precipitously.

View our latest analysis for ResMed

Click here to see the company's payout ratio, plus analyst estimates of its future dividends.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Businesses with strong growth prospects usually make the best dividend payers, because it's easier to grow dividends when earnings per share are improving. Investors love dividends, so if earnings fall and the dividend is reduced, expect a stock to be sold off heavily at the same time. That's why it's comforting to see ResMed's earnings have been skyrocketing, up 28% per annum for the past five years. ResMed looks like a real growth company, with earnings per share growing at a cracking pace and the company reinvesting most of its profits in the business.

The main way most investors will assess a company's dividend prospects is by checking the historical rate of dividend growth. Since the start of our data, 10 years ago, ResMed has lifted its dividend by approximately 8.2% a year on average. It's encouraging to see the company lifting dividends while earnings are growing, suggesting at least some corporate interest in rewarding shareholders.

Final Takeaway

From a dividend perspective, should investors buy or avoid ResMed? ResMed has been growing earnings at a rapid rate, and has a conservatively low payout ratio, implying that it is reinvesting heavily in its business; a sterling combination. Overall we think this is an attractive combination and worthy of further research.
